title: Quiche Lorraine
subtitle: The classic Alsatian bacon and cream tart
excerpt: Quiche Lorraine is a blind-baked shortcrust pastry case filled with smoked lardons, eggs, and cream. The original from the Lorraine region of eastern France contains no cheese: the filling sets as a smooth, just-trembling custard from the combination of eggs and cream alone.
sourceNotes: Quiche Lorraine originates in the Lorraine region of north-eastern France. The name comes from the German Kuchen (cake), reflecting the region's Franco-German history. The original version used bread dough; shortcrust pastry became standard in the 19th century. No cheese in the original.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze fully cooled, wrapped well. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat at 160°C fan for 15 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the day before, cool, and refrigerate. Reheat at 160°C fan for 15 minutes before serving.

content.text: The principle of quiche Lorraine is a custard set inside a pastry shell. The custard ratio is 3 eggs to 300 ml cream. Get that right and the filling will set to a smooth, barely-trembling consistency that slices cleanly. Blind-baking the pastry case before the filling goes in is not optional: it is what prevents a soggy base.
Roll the pastry out to 3 mm thick and use it to line a 23 cm loose-bottomed tin. Press firmly into the edges. Trim the overhang with a knife. Chill for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Line the pastry case with baking parchment and fill with baking beans. Blind-bake for 15 minutes, then remove the beans and paper and bake for a further 5 minutes until the base looks dry and pale gold. Reduce the oven to 180°C fan.
Fry the lardons in the butter over medium-high heat until golden and the fat has rendered, about 5 minutes. Tip into the pastry case and spread evenly.
Whisk the eggs and cream together with a generous pinch of salt, black pepper, and a little grated nutmeg. Pour over the lardons.

Bake at 180°C fan for 30 to 35 minutes until the filling is just set: it should still have a slight wobble in the centre when you gently shake the tin. Rest for 10 minutes before unmoulding and slicing.

items.cause: The pastry was not blind-baked long enough, or the filling was poured in while the pastry was still warm
items.fix: Blind-bake until the base looks completely dry. A small brush of beaten egg on the base after removing the beans (egg-wash blind-bake trick) and returning to the oven for 2 minutes creates a seal against moisture.

items.cause: Oven was too hot or the quiche was baked too long
items.fix: The filling is done when the outer 5 cm is set and the centre still has a jelly-like wobble. It will firm up as it cools.

items.symptom: Filling shrinks away from the pastry edges
items.cause: Normal with a custard filling. The custard contracts slightly as it cools
items.fix: Nothing to fix. This is expected. Avoid overbaking, which makes the shrinkage worse.

content.text: Lorraine sits between France and Germany. The quiche absorbed culinary traditions from both directions. The smoked pork (lard fumé) and cream filling reflects the region's proximity to Alsace and the German Rhineland, where pork and cream are central to the diet. The quiche Lorraine became the defining dish of French home cooking after the Second World War, when it spread throughout France and then to Britain and the United States.
